1156.title: The letters of the mind
1156.hook: a lesson that starts on the board and ends up inside: in the Patti, each school letter becomes a lesson for the soul
1156.howItsDone: In kirtan and katha the Patti is sung and explained stanza by stanza, and teachers draw out the inner lesson each letter carries, so a Gurmukhi letter becomes a reminder about the mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sasai: the One who fashioned the world is Master of all. Your line was he made it. A new week starts.

Some school lessons never stay at school. A teacher draws a number line on the board, and years later someone waiting on test results counts the days along it in their head. A coach says keep your eye on the ball, and it turns into advice about a marriage. The lesson leaves the classroom and moves inside. The Patti does that on purpose, letter after letter, and it says who the real student is.
screen: `A LESSON THAT LEAVES THE CLASSROOM.` → `IT MOVES INSIDE.` → `WHO IS THE REAL STUDENT?`

segments.voice: Start with the Patti's center line, its Rahao. It speaks to one pupil, and the pupil is the mind. In paraphrase: why do you forget, foolish mind? So the slate isn't really on a desk. It's inside. Now watch three letters turn a school lesson into a lesson for the soul. Kakai, the letter K. In paraphrase: when the hair turns white, bright without any soap, the messengers of death arrive and bind you in the chains of Maya. Guru Nanak makes the letter about gray hair in the mirror, and what it's quietly teaching. Dadai, the letter D. In paraphrase: I blame no one else; the blame lies in my own deeds. Whatever I did, that I received. Don't blame other people. On a school board, D is a shape to copy. In the mind, it's the hardest lesson there is: to stop pointing outward first. Tatai, a hard T. In paraphrase: why put on a show, mortal? In a moment, any moment, you may have to get up and go. Don't gamble your life away; run to the Lord's shelter. A child learns that letter by tracing it. The mind learns it by remembering it isn't staying forever. A school lesson is about the letter. A soul's lesson is about the one learning it. The Patti keeps both: you still learn your letters, but each comes with a question for whoever holds the pen.
screen: `THE STUDENT IS THE MIND.` · `KAKAI: WHITE HAIR TEACHES.` · `DADAI: BLAME NO ONE ELSE.` · `TATAI: YOU WON'T STAY FOREVER.` · then, large: `THE SOUL'S LESSONS.`

segments.voice: Think of something you learned as a child, share, look both ways, measure twice, and hold it as it was first taught. Then ask it the Patti's kind of question, what is this teaching the mind and not just the hands, so look both ways might become pause before I speak, and let one answer come without pushing for a clever one. If you pray, say Waheguru on the out-breath.
The letters of the mind. In the Patti, each letter turns a school lesson into a lesson for the soul, and the student the Rahao speaks to is the mind. Today's word.
screen: `THE LETTERS OF THE MIND — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the soul's lessons. Kakai, dadai, tatai: three letters, one pupil, the mind. On we go.

1157.title: The scholar's mistake
1157.hook: a person can recite the driving manual and still run the red light: the Patti says reading without living the letters is still not learning
1157.howItsDone: Sikh teaching pairs study of Gurbani with living it, often summed up as reading the Guru's word and then practicing it in daily conduct, seva and honest work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kakai, dadai and tatai: school letters turned into lessons for the soul. Your line was the soul's lessons.

A driving test comes in two parts. One happens at a desk, with a pencil. The other happens at a real crossing, with a real car coming. Someone can pass the first and fail the second, and only the second keeps anyone safe on the road. The Patti has a sharp line about which one counts, in the second half of its center line, the half we held back yesterday.
screen: `THE MANUAL, AND THE RED LIGHT.` → `KNOWING AND LIVING.` → `WHICH ONE COUNTS?`

segments.voice: Yesterday the Rahao spoke to the mind: why do you forget, foolish mind? Here's how it finishes, in paraphrase: when you give your account, brother, then you'll be counted as educated. The word for educated is parhiaa: one who has read. So the Patti redefines a reader. You haven't really read until you can give an account of your life. Not of the book. Of your life. That's the scholar's mistake: thinking the reading is the finish line. Second, the letter ngangai says it straight out. In paraphrase: whoever understands true wisdom, that one is the learned pandit. And the next line shows what that looks like: one who knows the One in all beings doesn't go around saying I, I. The proof of learning isn't how much you can recite. It's whether you see the One in the person in front of you, and let go of your own self-importance. Third, this isn't a poem against study. Guru Nanak put deep teaching on a schoolboard; the Patti honors the letters. It just won't let them stay on the board. Fourth, think about the account the Rahao means. Not a test score. A life story with the deeds left in. Did dadai make you blame less? Did tatai make you put on less of a show? Did sasai make you see one Master over everyone? That's the exam. A person who has never read a word could pass it. A person who has read everything could fail.
screen: `PARHIAA: ONE WHO HAS READ.` · `NGANGAI: WISDOM MAKES THE PANDIT.` · `NOT AGAINST STUDY.` · `THE ACCOUNT IS A LIFE.` · then, large: `LIVE THE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Pick one word from the Patti's letters, made, from sasai, blame no one, from dadai, or no show, from tatai, and think of one real moment in the hours ahead where it could show up: a meeting, a phone call, a line at the store. See yourself there, living the word instead of just knowing it, then let the picture go and rest with the breath. If you pray, say Waheguru once.

Your line: live the letters. The real exam is a life. Talk soon.

1158.title: Patti close
1158.hook: a wedding song remembered long after a grocery list: closing the Patti, an alphabet set in a raga and signed by Nanak the poet
1158.howItsDone: Ragis sing the Patti in Raga Asa as kirtan, returning to the Rahao line between stanzas, and some sangats sing it with children learning Gurmukhi so the letters and their meanings are learned together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the scholar's mistake: thinking reading is the finish line. Your line was live the letters.

A grocery list is gone from memory by the weekend. A song heard once at a cousin's wedding comes back years later with every word in place, because the tune held on to them. For four days this path has read the Patti as a tablet, as letters, as a lesson. It was always a song as well, with a raga to carry it. Today we close it by listening to it that way.
screen: `THE FAST MIDDLE PART.` → `THE TUNE CARRIES THE LETTERS.` → `THE PATTI AS A SONG.`

segments.voice: First, where it lives. The Patti doesn't sit in the Guru Granth Sahib as a school primer. It's placed in Raga Asa, among hymns that are sung, and its heading gives it a raga, which tells a musician how to sing it. The alphabet comes with a tune attached. Second, its refrain. The Rahao, the line we spent two days with, is the center the song keeps coming back to: why do you forget, foolish mind? When you give your account, then you'll be counted educated. Letter after letter moves forward, and the refrain pulls the mind back. That's how a song teaches. Third, how it ends. The last stanza says, in paraphrase: the One who made everything is doing all that is done, makes it happen, and knows it all. Thus says Nanak the poet. Saair, poet. Guru Nanak signs his alphabet not as a schoolmaster but as a poet. Fourth, look at what the song carried these last days: the tablet, and learning one mark at a time; sasai, the made world and one Master of all; the letters of the mind, gray hair, blame and the show we put on; and the scholar's mistake, that the real exam is a life. Read as a list, that's a lot. Sung, it's one thing: an alphabet turned toward God, with a tune to carry it until the heart can hold it alone.
screen: `SET IN RAGA ASA.` · `THE RAHAO PULLS THE MIND BACK.` · `THUS SAYS NANAK THE POET.` · `ONE ALPHABET, TURNED TOWARD GOD.` · then, large: `THE ALPHABET SINGS.`

segments.voice: Choose one letter's line, sasai, the One who made the world is Master of all, or dadai, I blame no one, the fault is in my deeds, and if you can, find a recording of the Patti in Raga Asa and listen for it. If not, hum the line softly three or four times to any simple tune, even two notes going up and down, then let it go quiet and sit with whatever stays. If you pray, end with Waheguru.
Patti close. Guru Nanak's alphabet, set in Raga Asa, carried by a refrain to the mind, and signed: thus says Nanak the poet. Today's word.
Your line: the alphabet sings. A tune holds what a list forgets. Rest easy.

1159.title: Words for a massacre
1159.hook: a tiger among the sheep: in Asa, Guru Nanak's hymn on the invasion asks the Master of the flock to answer for the ordinary people who suffered
1159.howItsDone: The Babarvani hymns are sung in kirtan and read in the Guru Granth Sahib like any other Gurbani; some Sikhs turn to them when remembering victims of violence and speaking about justice for ordinary people.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the Patti, signed by Nanak the poet. Today the songs turn heavy.

Two heavyweights step into a ring. Both trained, both chose to be there, and when one goes down, the crowd groans but nobody calls it a crime. Now change the scene. A tiger comes down a hillside into a field of sheep. Nobody chose this fight. The sheep can't hit back. Guru Nanak sang exactly that difference, about an invasion of Punjab, in a hymn in Raga Asa. Sikhs call his hymns on that invasion the Babarvani.
screen: `TWO FIGHTERS IN A RING.` → `A TIGER AMONG THE SHEEP.` → `THE BABARVANI.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Babarvani puts the name of Babur, the invader, beside vani, words: a small group of Guru Nanak's hymns about what Babur's armies did. One of them even uses the phrase for the invader's sway: Babar vaanee spread. Second, the hymn itself, in paraphrase. Khurasan is taken under the invader's hand, and Hindustan is put in terror. Then the Rahao turns to God: Creator, you are the Master of all. If the powerful strike the powerful, the mind holds no grievance. And the next verse holds the ring and the field together: but if a powerful tiger falls on a flock, the Master of the flock must answer for it. Guru Nanak doesn't grieve for kings losing to kings. He grieves for the flock: farmers, families, people who never chose a side and couldn't fight back. Third, notice where he takes that grief. Not to the invader, not to a crowd. To God, as the Master who is answerable. Earlier on this path we heard this hymn's cry, did you feel no pain? Today, hear the logic under it. If God is Master of all, the flock is God's flock, and its suffering is not a footnote. It is the point. Fourth, the hymn says the jewel of the land was spoiled, and no one cared for the dead. These are words for a massacre, kept in scripture and still sung, so the ones without power are remembered in the Guru's own voice.

segments.voice: Bring to mind people living through war today, not the leaders or the armies but the flock: a family packing in a hurry, a child at a shelter. If you pray, pray for them in your own tradition's way or say Waheguru on each breath out; if you don't, keep them in mind with each breath, as if sitting beside them. And if this touches a loss of your own and feels too heavy, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach your local emergency help.

1160.title: The women of Saidpur
1160.hook: a wedding photo in a ruined house: Guru Nanak's lament on ang 417 remembers the women as brides before it mourns what was done to them
1160.howItsDone: This ashtpadi of Guru Nanak in Raga Asa is sung in kirtan as part of Gurbani, and some Sikhs recall it when remembering those who suffered in war and partition.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Babarvani: a tiger falls on a flock, and the Master is asked to answer. Your line was he named the pain.

After a war, reporters walk through broken houses, and sometimes the camera stops on one thing left on a wall: a wedding photo. A bride in red, a groom beside her, everybody smiling. It says more than a casualty count. These were people with a before. In Raga Asa, Guru Nanak sings a lament for the women caught in the invasion. Tradition ties it to Saidpur, the town of Bhai Lalo. And before the hymn mourns, it does something unexpected. It remembers their weddings.
screen: `A WEDDING PHOTO ON A BROKEN WALL.` → `PEOPLE WITH A BEFORE.` → `A LAMENT ON ANG 417.`

segments.voice: First, the before. In paraphrase, the hymn says: those heads that were lovely with braids, the parting of the hair filled with vermilion. When they were married, their husbands looked handsome beside them. They came in palanquins decorated with ivory. Water was waved over their heads, and fans glittered beside them. Guru Nanak takes time over this. He lets us see them as brides, honored and celebrated. Second, the after. The same heads, the hymn says, are now shorn, and dust is in their throats. They lived in palaces, and now they're not allowed even to sit near. Strings of pearls are broken, and ropes are put around their necks. He doesn't go further into what was done. He doesn't need to. The before makes the after unbearable. Third, why tell it this way. A lament that only counted the dead would make them a number. This one makes them people, with their wedding day kept right beside their suffering. It's a way of mourning that refuses to let war shrink anyone. Fourth, who is speaking. Guru Nanak, a man, singing about women whose suffering could easily have been folded into someone else's story. He doesn't fold it in. He gives them stanzas of their own, set in scripture, where they are still sung and read. Not a footnote to the invasion, but people the Guru mourned with their before remembered.

1161.title: Truth to power
1161.hook: soft words for hard things: in Tilang, Guru Nanak speaks as the Word comes to him, to Lalo by name, and turns wedding words into plain words for killing
1161.howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Tilang shabad addressed to Bhai Lalo in kirtan, and its opening line about speaking as the Master's Word comes is cited as a model for honest, fearless speech.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the women of Saidpur, remembered as brides before the hymn mourns them. Your line was he mourned them.

Official language has a gift for soft words. An incident. Unrest. A regrettable loss. A difficult period. Each is true enough to say out loud and vague enough that nobody has to picture anything. Soft words protect someone. The question is who. Guru Nanak's hymn in Raga Tilang has no soft words in it at all, and it explains why in its very first line, spoken to a friend, Lalo, whom tradition remembers as a carpenter.
screen: `AN INCIDENT. UNREST. A LOSS.` → `SOFT WORDS PROTECT SOMEONE.` → `A HYMN WITH NO SOFT WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, the opening, in paraphrase: as the Word of the Master comes to me, so I speak it, Lalo. That's the hymn's whole method. It doesn't polish the Word into something safer. It says it as it comes. Earlier on this path we heard this line as courage, and later as truth told at the time of truth. Today, listen for its plainness. Second, the refrain. Line after line ends with ve Lalo, O Lalo. Plain speech here isn't a speech to a crowd or a letter to a palace. It's said to one man, a working man as tradition remembers him, again and again, the way you'd talk to a friend across a table when something terrible has happened. Third, the words it chooses. Yesterday the lament remembered weddings. This hymn uses wedding words too, and turns them inside out. The invader comes like a wedding party, but a wedding party of sin. Wedding songs are sung, but they're songs of blood, and blood takes the place of the red powder a bride wears. Every pretty word you'd use for a celebration is dragged into the light and made to say exactly what happened: a familiar word forced to tell the truth. Fourth, what that asks of us. Speaking truth to power, here, isn't shouting. It's refusing to blur: saying the thing as it is, to the person in front of you, by name, kindly, without letting the comfortable word cover it.

1162.title: Babarvani close
1162.hook: faith that doesn't look away from suffering
1162.howItsDone: The Babarvani hymns are part of the Guru Granth Sahib and are sung in kirtan and explained in katha, where they are heard as Guru Nanak standing with ordinary people who suffer in war.

segments.voice: Yesterday, truth to power: a hymn to Lalo with no soft words, the Word said as it comes. Today the hymns on Babur's invasion come to a close.

A nurse changing a dressing doesn't look away from the wound. She looks closely and steadily, because looking is part of the care. Turning away would be easier, and it would help no one. For days now this path has read Guru Nanak's hymns on Babur's invasion: the pain named, the women mourned, the truth told to Lalo. Today they close, with one question. What does a faith look like that keeps its eyes open?
screen: `A NURSE LOOKS AT THE WOUND.` → `THE PAIN NAMED, THE WOMEN MOURNED.` → `THE BABARVANI CLOSES.`

segments.voice: Babarvani is the name given to these hymns. Look back over what they do, and three things stand out. First, they look. They don't hurry a massacre into a tidy lesson. They stay with the dust, the broken homes, the ordinary people who paid for a war they never chose. The hymn on ang three hundred sixty even turns to God and asks, in paraphrase: there was so much slaughter, such crying, and did You feel no pain? Second, they keep calling God the Master. The same hymn names the Creator as the Master of all. Protest and trust share a single breath: a question like that is only asked of someone who is there. Third, they're kept. These aren't private notes hidden in a drawer. They sit in the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raga Asa and Raga Tilang, inside the same scripture that sings of joy and praise. A gathering can sing of the Beloved's beauty and, from the same pages, of a town that burned. So faith, in these hymns, isn't a way of looking away. It looks at the worst thing it can see, names it, grieves it, and brings the question straight to God, still saying God's name while it asks. That's today's line: faith that sees.
screen: `FIRST, THEY LOOK: THE PAIN IS NAMED.` · `GOD IS STILL CALLED MASTER.` · `THE HYMNS ARE KEPT IN SCRIPTURE.` · `FAITH THAT ASKS, AND STILL TRUSTS.` · then, large: `FAITH THAT SEES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one hard thing you usually glance past, far away in the news or close by, on your own street or in your own house, and just look at it for a few breaths without fixing it or explaining it away. If you pray, bring it to God plainly, as a question if it is one; if you don't, simply let it be seen. And if the hard thing is danger to you or someone close, reach for help now: 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
Babarvani close. The end of Guru Nanak's hymns on Babur's invasion: they name the suffering, grieve it, and still call God the Master. Today's word.
Your line: faith that sees. The Babarvani is closed, but its eyes stay open. See you tomorrow.
